nameStory: The Green Cloverworm Moth gets its name from its caterpillars, which are pale green 'worms' that love munching on clover and other plants in the pea family. Interestingly, this same species is also called the 'black snout' because of the dark coloring around its face area. It's a classic case of one moth earning two completely different common names based on different life stages and features!
description: The Green Cloverworm Moth is a small, brownish-gray moth with a wingspan about the size of a quarter to a half-dollar coin (roughly 1-1.4 inches across). Despite its name referencing green, the adult moth itself is actually quite drab, wearing muted earth tones that help it blend into bark and dead leaves. It belongs to a group of moths known for their triangular resting posture and slightly fuzzy appearance. You're most likely to spot these moths from spring through fall, and they're surprisingly common throughout New England.

idTips.label: Wing pattern and color
idTips.description: Brownish-gray wings with subtle darker lines and markings that create a mottled, bark-like appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: Forms a distinct triangular silhouette when at rest, with wings folded tent-like over its body rather than spread flat

idTips.label: Size reference
idTips.description: Wingspan roughly matches a quarter to half-dollar coin, making it noticeably smaller than many common sphinx or cecropia moths

idTips.label: Snout feature
idTips.description: Close inspection reveals a darker, somewhat projecting 'snout' area around the face, giving it the alternate name 'black snout'

idTips.label: Flight timing
idTips.description: Active from dusk into night, often attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting from March through November

habitat: Look for Green Cloverworm Moths in gardens, fields, forest edges, and suburban areas where their host plants grow abundantly. They're particularly common around areas with clover, beans, soybeans, and other legumes, but also frequent mixed woodlands where maples and cherry trees provide additional food sources for their caterpillars. These adaptable moths thrive from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in March and April, with fresh moths appearing at porch lights and outdoor fixtures during mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations overlapping. Both adults and green caterpillars are most abundant during warm summer months.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying through October and November until hard frosts arrive. Late-season moths may appear more worn and faded.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity in New England winters, though the species overwinters as pupae in soil or leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: This little moth accidentally became an international traveler when it hitchhiked to Great Britain hidden in a shipment of American soybeans, proving that even tiny moths can become globe-trotting stowaways!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small brown moths in the snout moth group, but the Green Cloverworm's triangular resting posture and moderate size help distinguish it from smaller grass moths or larger underwing moths. Remember: if it's triangle-shaped, quarter-sized, and brownish-gray, you're likely looking at a cloverworm moth.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you – while the caterpillars are green, the adult moths are brown! This common naming disconnect between larval and adult stages happens frequently in the moth world, where caterpillar characteristics often inspire the species name rather than adult appearance.
compareHints: The Green Cloverworm Moth is larger and more robust than its close relative the Baltimore Snout, which tends to be smaller and more delicate-looking. Green Cloverworms also have broader wings and a more pronounced triangular shape when resting, while Baltimore Snouts appear more streamlined. Both share the characteristic 'snout' feature, but the Green Cloverworm's overall bulkier appearance makes it the easier of the two to spot.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Green Cloverworm Moth, the Baltimore Snout is more brownish rather than greenish and has different wing markings.
